context: Starting at [0, 0] in a grid of nonnegative numbers, we can move only right or down. Let dp[i, j] be the minimum path sum to row i, column j, with indices starting at 0. The diagram shows the top-down brute-force recursion tree rooted at dp[2, 1], without specifying grid weights. Recursion looks backward to predecessors in the previous row and column, opposite to the downward and rightward moves of an actual path.

For a valid interior state, take the smaller predecessor result and add the current cell cost: dp[i, j] = min(dp[i-1, j], dp[i, j-1]) + grid[i, j]. The starting cell returns grid[0, 0], and an out-of-bounds negative index returns positive infinity.
description: The left branch of the recursion tree checks the previous row (“up”), and the right branch checks the previous column (“left”). The route labels describe directions in the grid, independently of the branches' positions in the drawing.

From root dp[2,1], going through dp[1,1] to dp[1,0] follows “up→left.” Going through dp[2,0] to dp[1,0] follows “left→up.” This illustrates the note at lower right: “dp[i+1, j] and dp[i, j+1] both depend on dp[i, j].” Here, dp[2,0] and dp[1,1] both depend on dp[1,0].

Brute-force search does not store solved states, so both calls to dp[1,0] expand the children dp[0,0] and dp[1,-1]. Negative-index nodes are labeled “Prune: index out of bounds.” The code returns positive infinity for them, excluding invalid predecessors when taking the minimum.

The symbolic 4×4 dp table below, with rows and columns indexed from 0 to 3, shades the six valid states visited: [0,0], [0,1], [1,0], [1,1], [2,0], and [2,1]. The other ten cells show their dp symbols but are not visited. The table below lists the entire recursion tree in call order: enter the node, check above, then check left. Different routes distinguish repeated states.

frames.explanation: The table contains 13 calls. The starting cell dp[0,0] occurs three times. There are four negative-index calls: dp[-1,1] once, dp[1,-1] twice, and dp[2,-1] once.

summary: When searching for the predecessors of dp[2,1], two call paths reach dp[1,0]. Its subtree expands twice, repeating the same calculation the second time.
